Kauhale Health plans memory care redevelopment
Kauhale Health recently announced the acquisition and planned redevelopment of a senior living community in Bluffton, South Carolina, according to a news release.
The Pines at Bluffton will be redeveloped into Kauhale Bluffton with a $5 million plan to turn the community into a memory care property that can serve 50 residents.
The redevelopment includes capital improvements, relicensing and repositioning the former assisted living and memory care property that first opened in 2000. The renovation effort is expected to last the next 12 months.
The acquisition is Kauhale’s fifth new property in four years.
55+ community planned in New Jersey
A former country estate will be developed into a new 55+ community by Garden Communities, according to a news release.
Ballantine Greens is under construction and the future community will include 250 one- and two-bedroom apartments with amenities. Offerings include one-acre village green with a pergola, walking paths, seating areas, a fresh-water pond, a gazebo, open green space and EV charging stations.
New community hits pre-sales milestone in Virginia
A new senior living community in northern Virginia has reached 100% occupancy in pre-sales nearly four years prior to opening, according to a news release.
Goodwin House Seminary Road is under development by provider Goodwin Living, and the community is planned to open in 2029 and span 257 apartment homes in a two tower construction.
The community will “primarily serve older adults through a continuing care Life Plan community model” but the development is allocating space for local housing affordability with designated units.
CopperWood Senior LIving plans construction start
CopperWood Senior Living, a new community in Peapack, New Jersey, will break ground on the development next month, according to a news release.
The community is set on 4 acres of land and will add over 200 units of independent living, assisted living and memory care. In August, investment bank Ziegler reported closing on financing for the luxury senior living development.
Construction: In Progress
Touchmark starts on Alaska community
Provider and developer Touchmark recently announced the start of construction on a new senior living development in the Anchorage, Alaska market, according to a news release.
Touchmark at Hillside will include 244 units and serve as Anchorage’s first full-service retirement community spanning independent living, assisted living and memory care. The 14-acre campus includes 120 condominium-style independent living homes, 34 villas, 58 assisted living apartments and 32 memory care homes in two secure neighborhoods.
“Alaskans shouldn’t have to choose between remaining connected to the place and lifestyle they love and having more choices for how they want to live in retirement,” said Marcus Breuer, CEO of Touchmark. “We see an opportunity in Anchorage to create something different: a community built first around living well and staying active, with the added confidence of knowing support is available if it is ever needed.”
Touchmark Development & Construction is leading the development and design of the community, working with a local team including Bettisworth North, Watterson Construction, DOWL, BBFM Engineers and T3 Alaska, with LRS Architects also providing architectural services.
Construction: Completed
Cedarhurst Senior Living finishes independent living expansion
Cedarhurst Senior Living recently announced the completion of 32 new independent living cottages at Cedarhurst of Frankfort in Frankfort, Illinois, according to a news release.
Construction on the cottages started in the spring of last year and all 32 cottages are now open, with move-ins underway. Cedarhurst of Frankfort also offers assisted living and memory care alongside its independent living component.
The cottages are designed for older adults that value privacy, independence and low maintenance living. Each cottage includes a two-bedroom floor plan with a zero-step entryway, walk-in closets, full-size kitchen appliances, laundry, private garage, a covered patio and a gas fireplace.
“Today’s older adults want choices that allow them to continue living life on their terms, and these cottages expand the living options we’re able to offer to meet those needs,” said Cedarhurst President Almir Sajtovic. “Our goal is to create an environment where residents can spend less time worrying about home maintenance and more time enjoying the people, experiences and opportunities that are meaningful to them.”
Residents also have access to a dedicated clubhouse that serves a weekly three-course menu and daily continental breakfast. Other amenities include a putting green, gym, athletic courts for bocce and shuffleboard.
Cedarhurst Senior Living announces Kansas community opening
Cedarhurst Senior Living also announced the opening of Cedarhurst of Shawnee, a new assisted living and memory care community in Shawnee, Kansas, according to a news release.
The two-story community spans 80,700 square feet on approximately 20 acres and includes 63 assisted living apartments and 26 memory care suites. The community is now accepting new residents.
Residents also have access to a movie theater, landscaped courtyards, housekeeping and laundry services, and wellness, social and recreational activities.
New affordable community opens in Florida
Riverbend Landings, a new affordable senior housing apartment community, recently opened and has reached 75% occupancy in Sanford, Florida, according to a news release.
The community includes indoor and outdoors spaces for resident recreation and wellness. On-site amenities include a waterside walking path, indoor and outdoor fitness facilities and a multi-purpose gathering space.

title: More Than Half of Primary Markets Have 90% Average Senior Living Occupancy Or Higher
description: Senior living occupancy is on track to reach record levels with more than half of primary markets reporting over 90% average occupancy. The national senior living average occupancy rate in the 31 primary markets NIC MAP tracks reached 90.4% in the third quarter of 2026, representing a gain of 60 basis points versus 2Q26, when […] The post More Than Half of Primary Markets Have 90% Average Senior Living Occupancy Or Higher appeared first on Senior Housing News .
content:
Senior living occupancy is on track to reach record levels with more than half of primary markets reporting over 90% average occupancy.
The national senior living average occupancy rate in the 31 primary markets NIC MAP tracks reached 90.4% in the third quarter of 2026, representing a gain of 60 basis points versus 2Q26, when average occupancy registered at 89.8%. The number of occupied units reached 644,428 in the third quarter of this year, a 70-basis point increase compared to 639,871 in the second quarter of this year.
Occupancy has risen across all senior living product types over the past quarter. Independent living average occupancy rose to 91.7%, up from 91.3%; assisted living rose to 89.1%, up from 88.3%; and active adult rose to 93.2%, up from 92.6%. Of the 31 primary markets NIC tracks, more than half, 16, are now at 90% occupancy or higher, up from 15 in the previous quarter.
Senior living construction continued to lag behind absorption in the third quarter. Senior living companies had a total of 16,159 units in development in the third quarter of this year while new inventory growth remained at 0.4% year-over-year, representing near record lows. Meeting the whole of senior living demand would require building more than 100,000 units annually through the 2030s, according to NIC MAP.
The senior living industry is on track to develop just 10,445 units per year, according to NIC MAP.
“The low levels of new supply being delivered when we are entering into a time when there is such opportunity and need ultimately hurts the customer,” Lisa McCracken, NIC’s head of research and analytics, told Senior Housing News. “We are hopeful that the conditions will change in a way that supports more development activity in a way that is a winning proposition for all parties.”
Over the past several quarters, NIC has seen a widening gap between what Baby Boomers will need and what the industry is producing, according to a press release.
“We’re hearing anecdotally that planning activity for new development is picking up, but until we see the trend reflected in the data, there will continue to be increasing pressure—and opportunity—to meet demand,” McCracken said in the release.
Arick Morton, CEO of NIC MAP, said new construction alone won’t get the industry to the level it needs, and the industry needs to consider “adaptive reuse of large buildings, expansion of existing properties or other creative ideas.”
McCracken told SHN that while adaptive reuse projects continue to be minimal within the market-rate developments, they are more common in affordable and subsidized projects.
“We think this is a significant opportunity if you can find the right property and location, particularly if aiming for a more middle-market type of option,” McCracken told SHN. “On the market-rate front, there are several projects whereby previously vacant mall properties are being repurposed into mixed-use developments and a market-rate 55+ component is being included.”
The Boston and San Francisco markets registered at 94% and 93.3%, respectively, representing near-record occupancy levels. The highest market occupancy NIC has ever recorded was 95.6%. Houston, Atlanta and Miami were the lowest-occupied primary markets with average occupancy rates of 87.3%, 87.2% and 86.5% respectively.
The active adult sector reached 93.2% average occupancy, representing a 1.3 percentage point increase since the end of 2025 and the highest occupancy for the product type since 2024. NIC MAP data “shows that fitness centers, clubhouses, pools and activity coordinators are the most common amenities in active adult communities, highlighting the role that wellness and social connection play in the appeal of this housing type,” according to the press release. Development for both active adult and multifamily has slowed, and the segment of the industry is working through a wave of supply that was completed over the past several years, particularly in the Sunbelt region.
Active adult occupancy reached 97.7% in Buffalo, New York and 97.4% in both Los Angeles and San Diego, while average active adult occupancy Phoenix registered at 88.7%.

title: How Soft Skills, Hospitality Focus Can Make Executive Directors More Effective
description: This story is part of your SHN+ subscription Executive directors are vitally important for senior living operators. The industry asks a lot of them, but I think there’s more support that operators can offer. From overseeing care coordination and delivering on lifestyle engagement that is increasingly focused on hospitality to keeping the number of incoming […] The post How Soft Skills, Hospitality Focus Can Make Executive Directors More Effective appeared first on Senior Housing News .
content:
This story is part of your SHN+ subscription
Executive directors are vitally important for senior living operators. The industry asks a lot of them, but I think there’s more support that operators can offer.
From overseeing care coordination and delivering on lifestyle engagement that is increasingly focused on hospitality to keeping the number of incoming move-ins and new hires flowing, the job of an executive director is not only crucial, but also hard. Simply put, an executive director must pick up the phone around the clock and leap into action when others can’t.
It’s simply a hard job at the end of the day, but I think that senior living operators can do more to support the leaders of their communities given how important the role is. While I think it is tempting to build airtight operating procedures and hold executive directors financially accountable, I think operators shouldn’t overlook “soft skills” like listening, communicating, coaching and building trust.
In practice, these soft skills are what I believe determine how residents experience a community and whether or not staff feel supported enough to stay long-term. And at the end of the day, I think these are the true drivers of a good senior living business, potentially more so than occupancy and margins.
Some companies seek out these skills by hiring leaders with hospitality experience, believing that the sector does a good job teaching these kinds of soft skills.
For example, Aegis Living has hired leaders with hospitality backgrounds and experience outside of senior living. General Manager and Partner Phil Clough joined Aegis in 2018 after nearly eight years with Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts and nine years with The Ritz-Carlton Hotel Company. To Clough, good service is not just following through on a plan but truly making someone feel welcome, which is not always an easy feat.
“It’s not just about executing; it’s about being the face of the community, dictating the ambiance and the culture and the welcome and the warmness of the community,” Clough told me.
In this week’s subscriber-only SHN+ Update, I examine why providers should develop soft skills and hospitality acumen and offer the following takeaways:
- Why providing good senior living customer experience requires more than just strong operational acumen on paper
- How providers are teaching communication and emotional intelligence with hospitality in mind
- Why leadership pipelines must also focus on hospitality, not only talent development
Good service means more than focusing on the numbers
To Clough’s point, I think senior living quality at its core hinges on helping residents feel well cared for, seen, respected and in control of their daily lives. Communities must combine personalization in services, enjoyable dining experiences and responsive problem-solving with meaningful social connection alongside quality healthcare services.
I believe certain hospitality principles lend well to senior living resident satisfaction and fit with the desires of prospective residents and their families. A 2022 analysis of Facebook reviews spanning 125 senior living communities by the Rosen College of Hospitality Management at the University of Central Florida found five factors that have the greatest impact on resident satisfaction. They include service quality and efficiency, physical environment, social environment, cost and amenities. When reviewers discussed healthcare, their satisfaction focused more on staff behavior than clinical expertise, the analysis found.
A hospitality-focused mentality belongs across all departments and should not be reserved for areas like dining or concierge services. Training of staff responsiveness and interpersonal behaviors to help residents feel supported will be vital in the coming years as older adults demand more from the communities they live in.
Seattle-based Merrill Gardens uses a hospitality-first strategy built around understanding resident preferences and family connections, including interviewing residents and creating profiles to help inform future programming and engagement. The provider connects residents with similar interests, and shared preferences are communicated to department leaders across communities.
I think learning resident interests and preferences is the bedrock for providers operationalizing hospitality within their communities. As Clough puts it, executive directors today must be “the face of the community,” able to dictate ambiance and culture and lead by example to create a welcoming environment for residents and staff.
“Bringing these skills linked with hospitality is a real and clear differentiator,” Clough told me. “You can build a beautiful community, but unless you have the heart and soul of the people that are within it, it doesn’t capture the heats and minds of families, and people can read right through that.”
First impressions matter for families seeking senior living options for their loved ones, and Clough told me that hospitality is the “real differentiator” in how families react to visiting a community for the first time.
“From a family’s point of view, if they put this much care into every detail of the building and the general manager is so visible and present, it gives them confidence their loved one will be incredibly well cared for throughout their time in the community,” Clough added.
Learning residents’ interests and their backgrounds is also vital. To improve engagement, providers can connect with former entrepreneurs, teachers, published authors, poets and artists to share their lived experiences and create meaningful programming opportunities or shared interest groups.
Applying these soft skills requires curiosity about who someone is and the ability to translate those connections into tangible engagement. To that end, it can help older adults retain their sense of purpose, and I believe it is up to operators to motivate community leaders to ask these simple but impactful questions.
Teaching leadership soft skills cannot stop after onboarding
Senior living providers need leadership candidates who already possess interpersonal competence and a tendency toward hospitality. Hiring for these traits is critical, and Atria Senior Living Senior Vice President of Human Resources Meg Pletcher told me some soft skills must be present when someone joins the company as a base for future on-the-job learning.
While training cannot make up for potential missteps in hiring, selecting a leader with a strong foundation of soft skills and interpersonal acumen will be critical going forward in finding the next generation of senior living executive directors.
Pletcher described Atria’s leadership development as an ongoing process, with relationship-building, empathy and judgment included in preparation for executive directors. She noted that technology “can’t inspire a team,” but can provide efficiency to staff that lets them spend more time connecting with residents.
This is critical as operators weigh adding new automation and business intelligence systems. While technology can give time back to community leaders, I believe the real value lies in what leaders do with that extra time. An executive director who gains time but lacks confidence in coaching an employee or addressing conflict may not automatically become more effective.
Pegasus Senior Living offers training that addresses conflict resolution, resident and employee satisfaction and emotional intelligence. The Dallas-based provider also helps executive directors evaluate stress and process frustration through regional leadership support to address persistent challenges in fostering a strong culture.
How an executive director handles pressure or conflict can influence how department heads respond to similar situations, which I believe makes teaching soft skills like composure and self-awareness essential to establishing the foundation for hospitality-focused practices to take hold at a community.
“Instead of running the building, they’re leading the community and developing the people who run the building,” Senior Vice President of People and Culture Katheryn Pigott told me.
This makes it important for providers to support executive directors so that they can become teachers and culture leaders for a community: individuals who can solve problems while also explaining the reasoning behind strategic decisions and remaining open to feedback when handling conflict or disruptive situations in the future.
If executive directors are expected to communicate, coach and create belonging, providers should teach those behaviors.
Leadership development must make hospitality more innate
I think the next step for senior living providers is to make hospitality a core part of an executive director’s skill set.
Senior Resource Group recently hired two executive directors with hospitality backgrounds. One of them dealt with a water pipe failure at a community and responded by proactively updating residents and families, apologizing for the disruption and explaining the community’s plan for addressing it, SRG COO Rob Henderson told me. He credited this proactive approach with helping the community move past the disruption.
To me, what matters in this situation is that the executive director did not wait for the problem to get resolved before addressing residents and families. Hospitality practices are easy to navigate when communities are operating smoothly, but I see the inherent value of these soft skills as having the greatest impact during times of disruption or inconvenience.
Providers should use these moments to prepare aspiring executive directors, and mentorship will be a critical piece of cultivating the next generation of senior living leadership.
SRG’s executive director in training academy provides a framework for this real-world experience and mentorship, with nearly half of the program consisting of rotating between departments to understand all aspects of community operations. Participants work with mentors to complete a “capstone” project addressing practical challenges SRG communities face.
Future executive directors should be able to explain not only how a department functions, but how its decisions affect the people living in the community. To that end, I think fostering and hiring leaders with these soft skills will be critical for success in the years ahead.

title: Polly want a pill?
description: We now live in a world where we self-diagnose, self-prescribe and self-administer medication-adjacent products all on our own.
content:
It’s such a cute word — polypharmacy. When I hear it, I think mostly of a very articulate parrot saying, “Polly want a cracker, and to experience potentially serious interactions from taking so many meds?”
According to a recent study reported in McKnight’s, polypharmacy — defined as the concurrent use of at least five medications or supplements — affects more than one-third of older adults. According to a second study, performed by me in front of my medicine cabinet, I’m one of them. So, possibly, are you.
It starts with the plethora of meds our primary care doctors and specialists prescribe for us, but it certainly doesn’t end there. We also have naturopaths, mental health nurse practitioners and an array of others potentially augmenting that regimen. We probably take additional vitamins and formulations that we may not have confessed to, or have forgotten to report, on our most recent medical check-ups.
And it doesn’t end there. We now live in a world where we self-diagnose, self-prescribe and self-administer medication-adjacent products all on our own. We see Instagram promotions and make impulse purchases, and embrace miracle cures recommended by friends or ChatGPT. Sometimes we even buy weight-loss meds from sketchy compounding pharmacies, draw them into a syringe and plunge needles into our stomachs while standing bleary-eyed at the kitchen counter.
So what does this mean for the folks being admitted to long-term care, or for each of us when we get there? It makes the job of the consultant pharmacist in a long-term care facility that much more important as a critical resource. As long as we report what we’re taking honestly, their expert Medication Regimen Reviews can help sort through all our badly researched choices and figure out what’s interacting with what and how much trouble it’s causing.
The weak link in the chain is us. The consultant pharmacist has visibility only to what the resident or family is disclosing and the facility is documenting. For example, if they don’t know about that multi-ingredient, Vitamin K-rich protein powder I’ve been taking every morning, they won’t know why my warfarin levels are so dangerously low.
In this new environment where everybody is their own doctor in a Wild West of self-diagnosis and marketing quackery, life for consultant pharmacists is bound to get a whole lot more complicated and essential.
And now we’re about to give them an even more impossible task than they ever imagined in pharmacy school — to save us from ourselves.
Things I Think is written by Gary Tetz, a two-time national medalist and three-time regional winner in the Association of Business Press Editors (ASBPE) awards program, as well as an Award of Excellence honoree in the APEX Awards. He’s been amusing, inspiring, informing and sometimes befuddling long-term care readers since the end of a previous century. He is a writer and video producer for Consonus Healthcare in Portland, OR.

title: 【高瀬比左子】介護の現場と経営、その「溝」を埋めるのは誰か ー 分断を越えて、同じ方向を向くために
description: 対話を続けていると、時々、昔から変わらない声が聞こえてきます。 現場からは、「経営者は数字のことばかり考えているように感じる。私たちが利用者さんのためにやろうとしていることを、分かってもらえない」。 一方で、経営者からは […]
content:
【高瀬比左子】介護の現場と経営、その「溝」を埋めるのは誰か ー 分断を越えて、同じ方向を向くために
対話を続けていると、時々、昔から変わらない声が聞こえてきます。
現場からは、「経営者は数字のことばかり考えているように感じる。私たちが利用者さんのためにやろうとしていることを、分かってもらえない」。
一方で、経営者からは、「現場には、事業を続けていくことの大変さがなかなか伝わらない。このままでは人件費も払えなくなる」。そんな声です。【高瀬比左子】
もちろん、すべての職場がそうだというわけではありません。経営者も、現場の大切さを分かっている。現場も、事業を継続することの大切さを分かっている。
それでも、日々の仕事の中では、お互いの見ているものが少しずつ違ってくる。同じ事業所で働いているのに、いつの間にか、別々の方向を向いてしまう。
介護の現場では、そんなすれ違いが起きているのではないでしょうか。
思えば、介護カフェを始めた十数年前にも似たような声を聞いていました。処遇改善の仕組みができ、介護職の賃金が社会的に大きく取り上げられるようになった頃も、
「経営者が何を考えているのか分からない」
「現場が何を求めているのか分からない」
という声はありました。
制度も介護を取り巻く環境も大きく変わりました。それでも、現場と経営の間にある「分かり合いにくさ」は、今もなくなってはいません。
これは、個々の事業所の問題だけではなく、介護という仕事が抱えている構造的な難しさの一つなのかもしれません。
◆ なぜ、すれ違いは続くのか
なぜ、これだけ長くこの溝が埋まらないのでしょう。介護カフェでさまざまな人の話を聞いていると、いくつかの理由が見えてきます。
一つは、そもそも「お互いの仕事を見る機会」が少ないことです。
現場の職員は、目の前の利用者さんへのケアや記録、家族対応、チーム内の調整などに追われています。一方、経営側には、人件費や稼働率、収支、採用、設備、事業継続など、現場からは見えにくい仕事があります。
経営者が現場を大切に思っていても、現場からは「数字しか見ていない」と見えることがある。現場が利用者さんのために頑張っていても、経営側からは「事業全体への影響が見えていない」と感じることがある。
どちらかが間違っているというより、見えている景色が違うのです。
もう一つは、使っている「言葉」が違うこと。経営側が使うのは、売上、人件費、稼働率、加算、収支、採用といった言葉。現場で交わされるのは、利用者さんの昨日と今日の違い、ご家族の表情、職員同士のちょっとした気遣い、ケアの難しさといった言葉です。
どちらも介護を続けていくために必要な情報です。ただ、それをつなぐ人がいなければ、同じ事業所の中にいながら、別々の言語を話しているような状態になってしまいます。
そして、その間に立っているのが、管理者や主任、リーダーといった中間層です。上からは経営側の考えを受け取り、下からは現場の声を受け取る。現場の気持ちも分かる。経営の事情も分かる。両方をつなぐ役割を期待されます。
けれど、その「間に立つ」という仕事は、決して簡単ではありません。
単に伝言するだけでは、どちらかの不満が残る。かといって、すべてを調整しようとすれば、その人自身が疲弊してしまう。
中間層の負担を考えるとき、人手不足だけでは説明できないものがあるように思います。
◆ 分断のままでいいのか
少し視点を広げてみると、介護事業所が抱えている課題の中には、一つの事業所だけでは解決しにくいものもたくさんあります。
人材確保。
賃金や人件費。
物価や光熱費の上昇。
制度改正への対応。
介護報酬の仕組み。
職員の育成。
地域の介護ニーズの変化。
こうした問題は、経営者だけが背負っても、現場の職員だけでも解決できません。
だからといって、「経営者も現場も同じ考えになろう」と言いたいわけではありません。立場が違えば、見えるものも、優先するものも違って当然です。
むしろ必要なのは、違いがあることを前提にして、「私たちの事業所にとって、今、本当に大切なことは何なのか」を一緒に考えられることではないでしょうか。
◆ カフェで見えてきた「つなぐ」ということ
介護カフェを続けていると、立場が違う人同士が同じテーブルにつくことで、少しだけ見え方が変わる瞬間があります。
普段は「経営者」として見ていた人が、家族や利用者さんとの思い出を話す。いつも「職員」として見ていた人が、事業を続けることへの不安を話す。
すると、「あ、この人も同じように介護のことを考えていたんだ」という瞬間が生まれることがあります。
もちろん、それだけで職場の問題が解決するわけではありません。対話をした翌日には、またそれぞれの役割に戻ります。
経営者は経営の判断をしなければならない。現場は利用者さんのケアに戻る。管理者は、その間で調整を続ける。
だから「一度話せば終わり」ではなく、話し続けられる仕組みが必要なのだと思います。
例えば、現場の職員が事業所のお金の流れや経営上の課題を知る機会があってもいい。経営側が、現場の仕事を実際に見たり、職員から日々の困りごとを聞いたりする機会があってもいい。
すべてを共有する必要はありません。でも、「自分たちの仕事が、事業全体の中でどうつながっているのか」を知るだけでも、見え方は変わるかもしれません。
そして、対話したことを「話して終わり」にしないことも大切です。
小さなことでいい。「まずこれを試してみよう」と決める。やってみる。その結果をまた話す。
そんな小さな循環があれば、対話は少しずつ職場の文化になっていくのではないでしょうか。
◆ 事業所の外に出てみる
もう一つ、私が介護カフェを続けてきて感じているのは、「職場の外に出ること」の意味です。
地域の別の事業所の人と話してみる。他の法人の経営者の話を聞いてみる。現場の職員同士で、「うちではこんなことがある」と話してみる。
すると、自分の職場で起きていることを、少し離れたところから見ることができます。
「うちだけの問題だと思っていたけれど、そうでもないんだ」と思えることもあります。逆に、「他の事業所では、こんなやり方をしているんだ」と新しい視点を得ることもあります。
地域の中に、立場や法人を越えて話せる場があること。それは、現場と経営をつなぐ一つの方法にもなるのだと思います。
◆ 現場と経営をつなぐのは、誰なのか
介護の仕事では、利用者さんの「できること」を一緒に探します。できないことだけを見るのではなく、「この人には何ができるだろう」と考える。
もしかすると、現場と経営の関係にも、少し似たところがあるのかもしれません。
「経営者は分かってくれない」
「現場は分かってくれない」
そんな風に、それぞれの「できないこと」に目を向けるのではなく、「この人と一緒にできることは何だろう」と考えてみる。
もちろん、立場が違えば意見がぶつかることもあります。
経営上、現場の希望をすべて受け入れられないこともあるでしょう。現場にも、事業全体の事情をすぐには理解できないことがあります。
だから、何でも分かり合う必要はないのだと思います。
違いがあるままでも、話せる。意見が違っても、共通の課題について考えられる。そのための「場」がある。私は、そこに対話の意味があるように感じています。
介護カフェを始めて十数年。いろいろな立場の人と話してきましたが、私自身もまだ答えを持っているわけではありません。だから問い続けています。
もし、あなたの職場で現場と経営が同じテーブルにつくとしたら、最初に何を話しますか。そして、そのテーブルをつくる人は、誰なのでしょう。
もしかしたら、経営者でも管理者でもなく、「一度、ちゃんと話してみませんか」と声をかけた、たった一人の職員なのかもしれません。
summary: 現場からは、「経営者は数字のことばかり考えているように感じる。経営者も、現場の大切さを分かっている。現場も、事業を継続することの大切さを分かっている。経営者が現場を大切に思っていても、現場からは「数字しか見ていない」と見えることがある。

title: 介護テック活用、在宅でも報酬で後押し　厚労省案　来年度改定で施設中心の評価から領域拡大　AIも含め検討
description: 来年度の介護報酬改定はひとつの転機になるかもしれない。テクノロジーの活用を後押しする評価が、これまで中心だった施設系サービスから在宅系サービスへ広がる公算が大きい。【Joint編集部】 厚生労働省は9月30日、来年度改定 […]
content:
2026年10月1日
介護テック活用、在宅でも報酬で後押し 厚労省案 来年度改定で施設中心の評価から領域拡大 AIも含め検討
来年度の介護報酬改定はひとつの転機になるかもしれない。テクノロジーの活用を後押しする評価が、これまで中心だった施設系サービスから在宅系サービスへ広がる公算が大きい。【Joint編集部】
厚生労働省は9月30日、来年度改定の「基本的な視点（案）」を審議会（社会保障審議会・介護給付費分科会）に提示した。
「居宅系サービスも含めたAIなどの介護テクノロジーの活用」を明記。例えば訪問介護や通所介護、居宅介護支援などの事業所を対象に、生産性向上の取り組みを介護報酬で後押しできないか検討する方針を示した。
背景にあるのは、深刻な人手不足とテクノロジーの進歩だ。職員の負担を軽減し、利用者への直接的なケアにより多くの時間を割ける環境を整えることで、サービスの質の確保・向上につなげる狙いがある。
具体策をどう講じるべきか、検討はすでに始まっている。厚労省は生産性向上に取り組む在宅系サービスの事業所を、加算で新たに評価することを俎上に載せている。今年8月の審議会では、考えられる評価のあり方を今後の論点として提示した。
来年度改定に向けて、講じる施策のアウトラインは年内に固める方針。在宅系サービスは小規模な事業所が多い。テクノロジーの導入・運用、加算の取得などに伴う負担を抑え、現場に取り組みが広がっていく制度設計も焦点となりそうだ。

content:
2026年10月1日
年間の介護費、過去最大12兆円超に 上位は特養、老健、通所 厚労省最新統計
厚生労働省が9月30日に公表した最新の統計（介護給付費等実態統計）で、昨年度の介護予防サービス・介護サービスの費用額が12兆2208億円となり、実績ベースで12兆円を超えたことが分かった。【Joint編集部】
前年度から2827億円、2.4％増加して過去最大となった。高齢化に伴う介護ニーズの拡大などが背景にある。
費用額は保険給付、公費負担、利用者負担の合計。福祉用具購入費や住宅改修費など、市区町村が直接支払う償還払いの費用は含まない。
年間に1度でもサービスを利用した人を数える「年間実受給者数」は、685万1600人。前年度から9万7600人、1.4％増えた。
介護サービスの費用額（介護予防サービスを除く）を類型別にみると、上位5つは以下の通りとなっている。
● 特別養護老人ホーム＝2兆1925億円
● 介護老人保健施設＝1兆3990億円
● 通所介護＝1兆3616億円
● 訪問介護＝1兆2820億円
● 認知症グループホーム＝7883億円
このうち特養は、地域密着型特養も含めると2兆4573億円となる。通所介護に地域密着型通所介護を合わせると、1兆7856億円で特養に次ぐ規模となる。

title: 【深層対談】介護AIに何を任すか　問われる人の役割と責任　NDソフト×BOS｜前編
description: 介護現場はかつて、テクノロジーの活用や生産性向上への関心が薄いと言われていた。もはや時代が変わったというほかない。【Joint編集部】 深刻な人手不足と膨らむ業務負担などを背景に、AIに対する期待がかつてなく高まっている […]
content:
【深層対談】介護AIに何を任すか 問われる人の役割と責任 NDソフト×BOS｜前編
介護現場はかつて、テクノロジーの活用や生産性向上への関心が薄いと言われていた。もはや時代が変わったというほかない。【Joint編集部】
深刻な人手不足と膨らむ業務負担などを背景に、AIに対する期待がかつてなく高まっている。活用の余地が大きいことは確かで、記録や議事録、シフト、ケアプランの作成などは一例に過ぎない。
こうした過渡期の只中で、介護ソフト業界を牽引するエヌ・デーソフトウェアの松山庸哉社長と、ブルーオーシャンシステムの寺岡正人社長の対談が実現した。
介護職員から経営者になった松山氏と、エンジニアとして第一線を歩んできた寺岡氏。異なる視座を持ち、本来はしのぎを削る競合関係にある2人が膝を突き合わせて語り合った。AIをなぜ使うのか、どう活かすのか、人は何を担うのか。
【PROFILE】
エヌ・デーソフトウェア株式会社 松山庸哉代表取締役社長。介護福祉士、社会福祉士、介護支援専門員の資格を持ち、介護職員、現場リーダー、施設長、エリア本部長、介護サービス法人役員を歴任。現場から経営まで一貫して介護に携わり、介護現場の課題解決、人材育成、DX推進を通じて、介護・福祉業界の発展に挑戦している。
株式会社ブルーオーシャンシステム 寺岡正人代表取締役。1991年より介護・障がい福祉分野の研究開発に従事し、厚生省研究事業に多数参画。ニューメディア開発協会主催メロー・ソサイアティーグランプリ受賞、AI分野の特許を先駆けて取得。1993年以降は特養のOA化研究事業に携わり、記録システムの開発で業界を牽引。1995年に富士ロジテックデータシステム（現ケアコネクトジャパン）へ転籍後、取締役開発部長、統括部長を歴任して業界の基盤構築に貢献。2010年に株式会社ブルーオーシャンシステムを設立し、介護現場に根ざした技術革新を推進。
◆ AIは介護現場をどう変えるか
寺岡：私はもともとエンジニアですので、既に日々の仕事でAIを頻繁に使っています。実際に触れていると、その力は非常に大きいと感じます。
今後、介護現場でも広く使われていくでしょう。松山社長は介護現場に実際に従事された経験をお持ちですが、AIの可能性をどう見ていますか。
松山：寺岡社長とは歩んできたキャリアが異なりますが、私も同様にAIのポテンシャルは非常に大きいと思っています。介護現場は人手不足が深刻です。職員を支え、生産性向上につながる技術は非常に重要でしょう。
寺岡：弊社でも早くから音声入力や多言語翻訳などの実装を進めてきましたが、生成AIの登場で可能性はさらに大きく広がりました。
松山：生成AIが出てきて、特に「言葉」を扱う力が大きく高まったと思います。介護現場には多くの事務作業があるので、この力をうまく活用できればインパクトは非常に大きいでしょう。
◆ 大切なのは「何のために使うか」
寺岡：気をつけなければならないのは、AIを導入すること自体が目的になってはいけないということです。
介護業界が向き合うべきは、人手不足の解消やケアの質の向上、利用者さんの生活の質をどう高めるかというテーマです。AIはこうした課題に対応する手段にほかなりません。
弊社では以前から、「気づく・学ぶ・つなぐ」というコンセプトをベースに製品を開発してきました。AIは、介護現場のそうした力をさらに広げてくれる技術だと捉えています。
松山：AIを活用する最大の利点は、職員が利用者さんと向き合う時間を増やせることですよね。人をAIに置き換えるのではなく、AIが人をサポートする。100の仕事をしていた職員が、AIの力を借りて150の力を発揮できるようなイメージを持っています。
寺岡：共感します。例えばスマートフォンのように、AIを使っているということを特別に意識しないまま、誰もが自然に使えるようになることも重要ですよね。置いてけぼりを出さず、介護現場に広く普及・浸透させる工夫が求められるでしょう。
松山：そうした変革の渦中で、どうしても避けられない論点が浮上します。何をAIに任せ、何を人が担うのか。ベンダーの我々が主体的に、介護現場を支える皆さんと共に考えていかなければいけません。
◆ 常に人が責任を持つ
松山：AIは優秀なパートナーですが、やはり責任主体にはなれません。常に人が確認して、人が判断して、人が責任を持つ。この原則は今後も変わりません。
例えば記録やケアプランなどは、AIに下書きを作ってもらうことができるでしょう。ただし、最終的に「これでいく」と決定するのは事業所、管理者、専門職です。
寺岡：大原則ですね。AIは間違うことがあり、入力内容によって全く違う答えが返ってくるものです。これを前提に人が責任を持つことが、まずは基本になるでしょう。
松山：例えばケアプランで言えば、AIがさらっと「答え」を書き上げてくれたとしても、それをそのまま採用してはいけません。「なぜその結論に至ったか」という根拠が非常に重要です。
利用者さんの状態や生活環境、意向などを踏まえて、本当に最も良い計画になっているのか。そこを考え、判断するのは常に人です。AIには、その判断を支えるパートナーであってほしいと思っています。
寺岡：「なぜその結論に至ったか」をクリアにする根拠として、例えば関連する介護記録が明示されるなど、システムに人がチェックするための機能が備わっていること、また、見つかったAIの間違いを人が簡単に修正できる機能が備わっていることが重要になります。
今後はもう一歩進んで、誰がどの段階で、どのようにチェックするかまで検討する必要があるでしょう。
議事録の場合、ケアプランの場合、事故報告書の場合など、それぞれ人がどう介入するのがベストなのか。そうした手順自体を設計することが重要になっていきます。
松山：そうですね。何をAIに任せ、どこから人が責任を持つべきか。私たちベンダーが正しく伝えることも大切になっていきますね。
▶ 後編では、AIへの過度な期待を煽らない情報発信のあり方と、ベンダーの競争・協調に迫る。

content:
2026年9月30日
厚労省「介護現場は厳しい」 来年度改定、目玉に物価高への対応や賃上げ 経営の安定へ財源確保が焦点
来年度の介護報酬改定の大方針が示された。大きな柱はやはり、物価の上昇や他産業で進む賃上げに対応すること、介護従事者の処遇改善を一段と進めることだ。【Joint編集部】
厚生労働省は9月30日、来年度改定の「基本的な視点（案）」を審議会（社会保障審議会・介護給付費分科会）に提示した。
物価・賃金の上昇などで経費が膨らんでいることを踏まえ、「介護現場は厳しい状況に直面している」と認めた。全サービスの赤字事業者の割合が約4割にのぼる、という昨年度の深刻な調査結果も紹介した。
厚労省はそのうえで、「物価や賃金の上昇などを介護報酬に適切に反映し、事業者の経営の安定を図る」と明記した。あわせて、介護従事者の「他職種と遜色のない処遇改善」を実現し、人材の確保・定着や離職の防止につながる環境を整備する考えも示した。このほか、職場環境の改善と生産性向上も柱のひとつに据えている。
一方、制度の安定性や持続可能性の確保にも言及した。
ここでは、「特に現役世代を中心に、保険料負担の増加に対する懸念が示されている」と指摘。限られた財源を有効に活用していく必要があるとして、「介護報酬の評価の適正化・重点化を進めるとともに、報酬体系の整理・簡素化を図る」と掲げた。
今回の「基本的な視点（案）」は、今秋から佳境へ向かう来年度改定の議論の羅針盤となる。事業者の経営の安定と介護従事者の賃上げを支える財源を得るために、必要な負担へのコンセンサスや納得感をどう形成するか。今回も、この問いへの答えが鍵を握りそうだ。

description: 厚生労働省は9月28日、来年度の障害福祉サービス報酬改定に向けた議論を進めている有識者会議（障害福祉報酬改定検討チーム）で、就労系サービスの具体策を取り上げた。【Joint編集部】 事業所の新規指定や運営の指導に関する既 […]
content:
厚生労働省は9月28日、来年度の障害福祉サービス報酬改定に向けた議論を進めている有識者会議（障害福祉報酬改定検討チーム）で、就労系サービスの具体策を取り上げた。【Joint編集部】
事業所の新規指定や運営の指導に関する既存のガイドラインを厳格化する案を提示。確実に実施すべき事項を、就労系サービスの施行規則や指定基準などに位置付けることを提案した。
こうした提案の背景には、ガイドラインの整備だけでは自治体が事業所に強制力をもって働きかけることが難しいとの指摘がある。
厚労省は会合で、既存のガイドラインを厳格化して、就労系サービスの施行規則や指定基準などに位置付ける主な分野の案として、
● 指定申請書・事業計画書について
● 収支予算書について
● 生産活動について
● 在宅支援について
などを提示。このうち生産活動については、
● 具体的な生産活動を行い、一般就労に必要な能力の向上と安定した生産活動収入が見込まれること
● 習得した能力を活かせる労働市場や求人が地域にあること
● 生産活動以外の訓練カリキュラムについて、サービス提供時間に占める割合が過大とならないこと
●「生産活動シート」を作成し、運営指導や指定更新、毎年度初めの届出時に指定権者へ提出するとともに、ホームページで公表すること
といった事項を、施行規則や指定基準などに位置付けることを提案した。

title: 就労B型、生産活動の収支を工賃の総額以上に　指定基準の見直し案｜障害福祉報酬改定
description: 厚生労働省は9月28日、来年度の障害福祉サービス報酬改定に向けた議論を進めている有識者会議（障害福祉報酬改定検討チーム）で、就労継続支援B型の具体策を取り上げた。【Joint編集部】 「生産活動の収支が利用者に支払う工賃 […]
content:
厚生労働省は9月28日、来年度の障害福祉サービス報酬改定に向けた議論を進めている有識者会議（障害福祉報酬改定検討チーム）で、就労継続支援B型の具体策を取り上げた。【Joint編集部】
「生産活動の収支が利用者に支払う工賃の総額以上となること」を指定基準に位置付ける案を提示。現行、就労継続支援A型には同様の規定があるがB型にはない。
就労継続支援の指定基準では原則、賃金・工賃の支払いに自立支援給付を充ててはならないと定められている。厚労省は会合で、提案の趣旨を以下のように説明した。
「就労継続支援B型でも、生産活動収支が賃金総額を下回っている場合には、適切な支援を行うための報酬（自立支援給付）が賃金に充てられており、利用者に安定的なサービスを提供しているとは言えない」
厚労省はあわせて、運営法人の資金や寄付などから利用者に金銭を支払った場合について、その額を基本報酬の算定に用いる平均工賃月額から除く案も示した。

content:
OpenAI DevDay 2026 live blog
29th September 2026
I’m at OpenAI DevDay today, in Fort Mason, San Francisco. Same as last year I’ll be live blogging the keynote and some other notes during the day.
OpenAI gave me a free ticket and a seat in the “creator” area for the keynote.
09:27 I'm in the room for the keynote, which starts in half an hour.
This year I vibe-coded a system for more easily adding photos to my live blog. I intended to do that using Codex Cloud (I built it on my phone on the way to the venue) but ran into problems with that and switched to Claude Code for web instead.
10:01 Sam Altman is on stage, welcoming us to DevDay. He promises "our best DevDay yet".
10:02 Showing features they've shipped that people asked for. Codex on Linux and Codex on your phone both got some applause.
10:03 Today, a product to feel like a "whole new way of working with AI". My guess is that it's a personal agent similar to Muse...
10:03
10:03 It's called "Dots".
10:05 It does look very Muse-like. You get to pick its name, then it's represented by a cute blob-like avatar. (My Muse avatar is a pelican.)
10:06 This demo video includes a whole lot of voice interactions, presumably using GPT-Live or a new generation of that technology.
10:06
10:07 Dots are "powered by Astra". That would be an expensive default model!
10:08 A very ambitious use-case, migrating an API. I'm surprised that they went for such a code-heavy example so early on, I guess this is a developer audience.
10:09 Sam called Astra "our most aligned model", to allow you to trust your Dot with "as much responsibility as you are comfortable with".
10:09 "You also need a place four your team to collaborate with their Dots". So they are introducing ChatGPT Space.
10:10
These Spaces look like shared artifacts, maybe Google Docs meets the artifacts pattern.
Sam Introduces Holly Li.
10:11 Holly is talking through a scenario building fictional music app. Holly has a Dot called "Dottie", which has access to ChatGPT, Slack, Teams, and more.
10:12 This UI really does look like Meta's Muse agent, currently still at number one on the iOS App Store free list.
10:13 Live demo! "Dottie is having a slow morning" - we got a "still checking" and an embarrassing silent moment.
10:14 Now we're in ChatGPT Space. It has a Notion-style slash menu.
10:16 People at OpenAI started delegating to their Dots directly in Slack, which have their own identities in OpenAI Slack. I guess this is OpenAI's answer to Claude Tag.
10:17 "Dottie can use Codex on my laptop to build the app and launch it in the iPhone Simulator."
10:18 ChatGPT Pro and Enterprise customers get access to Dots today.
10:19
10:19 They're also building "specialist dots" for legal, finance, etc. They'll collaborate with enterprises on this, and are also doing a thing with Microsoft 365 around these.
10:20 "The second big part of today" is about platforms. Says says: Great models. Tools - access to the same tools used within OpenAI. And distribution.
10:21 People have been asking for GPT-6 Astra but cheaper and faster. Today they're launching GPT-6.1 Sol.
10:21 "Near-Astra level intelligence at a fifth of the price".
10:22 6.1 Sol is launching by today.
10:22 Also today: Ultrafast. 8x faster - up to 300 tokens/second. Available in the API, ChatGPT, and Codex. 6x the price of standard - "you know what, it's worth it" says Sam.
10:22 Ultrafast is available for Astra 6 today, and Sol 6.1 soon.
10:23 New subscription plan: Pro 500. This gives you access to Ultrafast, and 25x the usage of Plus. They're also putting their $200/month plan back on sale for new subscribers today.
10:24 Also today: previewing a new Decisions API. Lets the model respond "in a fraction of a second". It works by giving the Luna model "a predefined set of options to choose from". Sounds like their response to Jev, which came out of stealth less than two weeks ago!
10:25 Sam is now talking about Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI. He brings up Tejal Patwardhan to talk about how they're using their own models to accelerate their research.
10:26 Tejal is talking about Astra's abilities at Computer Use. "Our models helped optimize the harness we use for Computer Use". They accelerated the harness, getting "a 2x latency win that we've shipped to all of you".

15:11 The backend had GPT-6 Astra writing code to draw the images.

15:22 They finished by asking Marin to generate some images.
15:26
Here's Getting started with GPT-Live and the openai-live-console starter app on GitHub.

15:38 That kicks off at 4pm, in about 20 minutes.
16:00 (As an aside, there are some excellent California Brown Pelicans flying around the bay near the event venue today. Glad I brought my camera!)
16:04 This closing session features Sam Altman, Thibault Sottiaux, and Tejal Patwardhan (a late addition, not listed in the program). The moderator is Pauline Narvas.
16:06 Sam says "we should have done it a long time ago" about Sign in with ChatGPT.
16:09 GPT Astra has been surprisingly competent at operating robots. Sam says this has updated his timeline for when we'll have people "building really cool robots".
16:10 (I'll be honest, this Q&A has been pretty flat so far - the questions are such low-balls, "how do you see dots in the next year", "why should developers be excited about Sign in with ChatGPT" kind of things.)
16:12 Q: What's something people should start building now that models can't do but should be possible by DevDay next year?
Sam: I would expect next DevDay to feel unimaginable if we can get alignment right so we can keep training. Tejal doesn't like to predict three months in advance. Sam "I did not think we would prove a millennium prize problem within a year of the last DevDay". Thibault thinks next year we'll have deep 3D understanding and multi-modal input.
16:14 Q for Tejal: what can today's models do well on a benchmark that they still struggle with in the real world? Professional writing copy, not writing AI slop. Being faster, better at reading context. "A lot of the intelligence improvements we need for more ambitious projects are there."
16:15 Thibault says me thinks people are hitting decision fatigue over when to use subagents, what reasoning level to make. "In six months we'll get back to the simplicity of a system that actually understands what you need".
16:17 Community question about the job market - what advice do you have for a college graduate today? Sam: I think this is a great time to enter the job market. Many job categories that exist today will be very different or won't exist - but the AI industry has underestimated how much human demand and expectations will go up. People use want way more software, and what it means to be a coder has changed. "I have never seen startups be more successful as a whole than in this last year." If you are an ambitious person graduating college right now this is the best time.
16:17 Tejal calls for college students to work on alignment and safety!
16:17 Thibault says "my favorite colleagues right now are the new grads at OpenAI". Grounded ideas and good taste.
16:18 Pauline promotes the Codex Ambassadors program, says that getting involved in events (and running events) is always a good idea.
16:20 Thibault talks about how dots came out of the Codex harness getting more reliable and being able to handle longer tasks. Also says that Ultrafast has "made building impossible things possible" - they used that to help merge the ChatGPT desktop and Codex desktop apps in 28 days. Everyone on stage loves Ultrafast.
16:20
16:22 Community question about agent-to-human bandwidth, as the amount of information continues to increase. Tejal says that they've been talking about how agent-to-agent communication should differ from agent-to-human, and potentially post-training for those two differently.
16:23 Sam mentions the idea of agents creating custom UI for you in real-time.
16:25 Thibault likes using Pi! He says it helps understand the fundamentals, and loves that it can coexist alongside Codex.
16:26 Sam says you need to build a business with durable advantages, same as always. (And that OpenAI will help you do that with their new distribution efforts.)
16:28 Q: How should developers think about the relationship between token costs and usage limits? Thibault says 6.1 Sol is incredibly efficient. They need the economics to make sense on the plans. The thing they care about is how many tasks you can get done through your subscription, not token usage. Likes to see people talk about "outcome per dollar".
16:29 Community question: How do you find the builders who don't know they are builders yet? Sam says that coding agents are much harder to get going with than ChatGPT, unifying Codex and ChatGPT helped more people become builders, but now hopes that people can talk to their dot during the day and that dot will then go away and build things and be helpful.
16:31 Thibault: maybe next day we'll rename it to BuildDay, not DevDay. Also your dot knows what it looks like and can use Blender, so it can render little scenes featuring itself. "Everyone will become a builder. Everyone will create. Developers will also turn into builders - and manual development of code isn't really something that will exist."
16:32 Q: At what point will the models be so good that all the live demos work? (There were a whole lot of demo failures during DevDay). Sam: we take pride in demoing things when we launch them, and I'm proud that we take the risk on this.
16:34 Q: As agents start working how do you decide when they should act on your own and when they should check with us? Thibault: dots don't have access by default to everything you have shared with ChatGPT already. You can give it as much responsibility and goals as you are comfortable with.
16:38 Sam is excited about what the next generation of models will be able to do with mechanical and electrical engineering, in the same way that Astra made big leaps in robotic control.
16:40 Question about pacing the frontier. What will you do to pace the frontier and get out of those race dynamics and make sure AI is safe for all of us? (applause)
Sam: No matter what governments do we will work to keep AI safe. There will be times like right now when we need to put more effort into increasing our capabilities there before we increase the model capabilities in a traditional sense.
16:42 Panel is over!

content:
2026年9月29日
カイポケ、会話から記録を自動作成するAIと連携 訪問看護で先行 ケアマネや訪問介護、福祉用具も対応へ
介護事業所の経営を支援するクラウドサービス「カイポケ」が、ケア中の会話から業務記録を自動で作成するAIツール「スタンドLM」との連携を始めた。【Joint編集部】
9月17日から訪問看護向けに正式提供し、10月には居宅介護支援にも対応する予定。エス・エム・エスは9月、スタンドLMを手がけるENBASEと戦略的パートナーシップを締結した。
スタンドLMは、訪問先の利用者宅などの現場で交わされた会話をAIが解析し、サービス種別や事業所の書式に合わせて業務記録を自動で作成するツール。例えば、サービス担当者会議や各種カンファレンスの議事録、モニタリング記録、サービス提供記録、支援経過記録、多職種への報告文章などの作成を効率化できる。
訪問看護、訪問介護、居宅介護支援、福祉用具貸与などに対応。蓄積された記録をもとに、計画書や報告書の作成につなげる機能もある。
先行して連携が始まった訪問看護では、例えば、アプリで録音した会話をもとにAIが「看護記録Ⅱ」を作成。職員は内容を確認したうえで、ワンタップの送信でカイポケに登録できる。
こうしたカイポケとスタンドLMの“ワンタップ連携機能”は、10月に居宅介護支援、年内に訪問介護へ広がる予定。その後、福祉用具貸与にも拡大されていく。
エス・エム・エスは、「両社サービスの特長を掛け合わせることで、カイポケの機能的な付加価値を高めていく。在宅サービスの業務効率化の支援をより一層強化していく」としている。

content:
2026年9月29日
介護福祉士養成校の入学者、外国人留学生が初の6割超に 638人増で全体を押し上げ
介護福祉士を養成する大学や専門学校などで組織する「日本介護福祉士養成施設協会」は29日、今年度の入学者の動向を公式サイトで発表した。【Joint編集部】
それによると、外国人留学生は前年度より638人多い4712人となった。入学者の総数に占める割合は60.6％で、初めて6割を超えた。
※ 記事中の人数や割合などは、協会の調査に回答した会員養成施設の集計値。
入学者の総数は424人増の7780人。新卒者らは177人減の2756人、離職者訓練の受け入れは37人減の312人だった。外国人留学生の伸びがこれらの減少を補い、入学者の総数を押し上げた格好だ。
外国人留学生の出身国はネパールが2539人で最も多く、単独で半数以上を占めた。次いでミャンマーが904人、ベトナムが377人となっている。
定員の充足率は前年度の66.9％から73.6％に上昇した。一方、養成課程数は272から266に、入学定員は1万1001人から1万572人に減少した。

沖縄・渡名喜島唯一の保育所始動 人材難で５年間開所できず
2026年09月29日 福祉新聞編集部人口３００人弱の沖縄県渡名喜島で保育所が今夏開所した。保育士を募集しても応募がなく人材確保が難航し、「ハコだけがある状態」が５年間続いていた。今年度保育士ら３人を採用できたことで、島唯一の保育所が動き出した。
渡名喜村ではこどもが１～２人生まれる年もあるという。村立幼稚園があり、３～５歳児を受け入れるが、保育所はなく０～２歳児の預け先がない状況が続いており、村はかねて受け皿の確保を模索してきた。
老朽化した老人福祉センターを建て替えて整備した、同村社会福祉協議会による通所介護や、民俗資料館が入る「多目的拠点施設」の一室（９０平方メートル）に小規模保育所を設けた。
ハコができても保育士ら必要な職員を配置しないと、こどもを受け入れることはできない。２０２１年度から、ハローワークや村ホームページで求人を出すなどして保育士募集をスタート。しかし、２４年度に至るまで応募が１件もなく開所できない状況が続いていた。
２５年度からは、沖縄県保育士・保育所総合支援センターの合同就職説明会に参加したり、内閣府の離島活性化事業を活用して保育士の移住に係る引っ越し費用を補助したりするなど採用に力を入れた。こうした中、人手不足で保育所が開所できないとの地元メディアの報道から、村外出身の保育士１人から応募があった。今年度、村立幼稚園に通うこどもがいないため、退職予定だった保育士１人、保育補助１人を会計年度任用職員として採用し、小規模保育所の開所にこぎつけた。
８月３１日に開所式があり、現在１歳児１人が通う。定員は１９人だが、現状の職員配置では５人が上限だという。村の担当者は「子育て世帯が島に移住したくても、安心してこどもを生み育てる環境がなければ躊躇してしまう」と指摘し、これまでなかった保育所の開設を契機に移住促進に期待を寄せている。

content:
厚生労働省は28日、来年度の障害福祉サービス報酬改定に向けた議論を進めている有識者会議（障害福祉報酬改定検討チーム）で、就労継続支援や就労移行支援の在宅支援を取り上げた。【Joint編集部】
在宅支援を提供できる利用者と事業所の要件を厳格化する案を示した。
厚労省は会合で、
● 在宅支援と称して、公費による就労支援の生産活動として適さない活動
● 就労に必要な知識・能力の向上に寄与しない自習
を行わせているなど、「就労支援の実態が認められない不適切な運営がある」と問題を提起。在宅支援が認められる際の要件を、より具体的に設定することを提案した。
利用者の要件については、単に在宅支援の効果が認められる人ではなく、「通所を上回る効果が認められる人」とする案を提示。その対象者として、
● 重度の障害や地理的な要因で通所が困難な人
● 通所支援を行うために、まず在宅支援が必要な人（ひきこもりなど）
● 在宅での一般就労を希望し、自立・集中して作業ができる人
の3類型をあげた。厚労省はこのうち、在宅での一般就労を希望する人に対する在宅支援の提供は、原則として就労移行支援に限ってはどうかとした。
事業所の要件については、対象者に応じた支援プログラムの提供や緊急時の対応、本人のアセスメントなどを求めることを提案。支援の状況を動画などで保存し、自治体の求めに応じて提出できるようにすることを必須とする案も示した。
厚労省はあわせて、在宅支援の基本報酬を一定程度引き下げること、定員に占める在宅支援の利用者の割合に上限を設けることも提案した。従来の単位数を維持し、利用者の割合に上限を設けない要件としては、
● 在宅の利点が活かされる高単価の生産活動を行っている（動画・ホームページ作成、プログラミングなど）
● 在宅でなければできない訓練が適切かつ確実に提供されている
● 動画やバーチャル環境で利用者と常にコミュニケーションを取れる環境が整備されている
などをすべて満たすことを求めてはどうかとした。
厚労省はこのほか、事業所に「在宅支援の内容に関するチェックリスト」を事前に提出させ、自治体が確認できるようにする流れも説明した。自宅以外での在宅支援の利用は、「極めて限定的な場合に限る」との考えも示した。
今後、来年度改定の大枠の方向性を固める年末に向けて、具体的な要件・報酬などを詰める検討をさらに進める方針だ。

content:
〈村山誠厚労事務次官インタビュー〉介護・障害報酬改定、他職種と遜色なく
2026年09月28日 福祉新聞編集部厚生労働省の村山誠事務次官は８日、２０２７年度の介護報酬、障害報酬改定について「賃上げの状況や経営実態に即した対応がとれるよう実態調査を含め、きちんと積み上げを行い、他職種と遜色のない処遇改善の実現につなげたい」と語った。
同日、厚生日比谷クラブ加盟社による共同インタビューで答えた。物価高により医療や介護の現場は厳しい経営状況にあるとの認識も示した。「他職種と遜色のない処遇改善」は２５年と今年の政府の骨太の方針に明記されている。
熊本地震
個別訪問による在宅の方の健康状態の把握、車中泊の方の熱中症やエコノミークラス症候群の注意喚起、予防指導などの取り組みを進めてきた。
８月２７日に政府全体の支援パッケージを決定し、関連の予備費の使用も翌日に決めた。今月４日は本部会議に衣替えし、これから復旧・復興支援に軸足を置くフェーズになっている。
外国人
社会保障はじめ各種制度を外国人に伝えるのが難しい。日本語をめぐる問題が大きなテーマだ。労働施策総合推進法に基づく事業主向けの外国人雇用管理指針を先般改訂したが、日本語学習支援も事業主の責務だと明記した。
やさしい日本語、多言語による周知を、一層の取り組みを進めていく必要がある。
労働力確保
高齢者は６５歳までと同じようにノルマとかではなく、慣れた仕事を週に何時間か確実にこなす、そこならやりがいをもって働けるという面もある。
みんなが１日８時間労働するのでははなく、仕事を切り出していけば、特に７０代以降は労働参加が進む余地はあるのではないか。
エッセンシャルワークは一定以上の高齢者がスキルを生かしながら軽い負担で経験を生かす形をつくることが大切ではないか。

2026 in LLMs (so far)
27th September 2026
On Friday I gave the closing keynote at the WeAreDevelopers World Congress North America in San Jose. I tied together the key trends from the past year into a chronological exploration of everything that happened in 2026. The video is on YouTube; here are my annotated slides and notes to accompany the talk.
And as an annotated presentation:
I’m going to give a lightning tour of everything that has happened so far in 2026. The year isn’t over yet!
For me, 2026 started a couple of months earlier in November 2025.
November saw the release of two important models: Claude Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1.
As is usually the case with new models, these were incremental improvements on the models that came before them.
But every now and then when a model improves, it crosses an invisible line where something that didn’t really work starts working.
In this case, the thing that started working was their coding agents. Claude Code had been around since February 2025; Codex was a little younger.
These two new models, when paired with their respective coding agent harnesses, improved from “often make mistakes” to “reliable enough to use on a day-to-day basis”.
For a couple of years now I’ve been evaluating new models by asking them to “Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle”. It’s probably the world’s stupidest benchmark—there’s only so much you can learn from it.
But it’s still a challenge for models, because drawing pelicans is difficult, drawing bicycles is difficult, and pelicans can’t ride bicycles in the first place.
Here’s the state of the art for November. Claude still couldn’t really draw a bicycle! The GPT-5.1 bicycle frame is pretty crap too.
Also in November, we had the first commit to an obscure GitHub repository called “Warelay”. We’ll come back to this repository shortly.
And then there were the December holidays, and individual developers took some time off and many started tinkering with these new coding agent model combinations... and it began to dawn on us quite how much they could do that they couldn’t do before.
Come January, a lot of us were quite excited to start putting this stuff into action.
Every year I set myself a New Year’s resolution, and for as long as I can remember it’s been the same thing: stay focused. Take on less new projects. Try to get things done in the projects I already have.
This year I decided that since that had never worked before, I’d go the other way.
We’ve got coding agents now, let’s see what they can do. I’m going to take on as many new projects as I like!
(You can ask me at the end of the year if this turned out to be a good idea or not. I have a lot of plates spinning right now.)
“Be more ambitious” has been something of a theme for the year, because the only way to find the limits of this technology is to keep on pushing them until they don’t work.
I also went on the Oxide and friends podcast with Bryan Cantrill and Adam Leventhal to share predictions for the next year (and three and six years).
With hindsight, my LLM predictions were pretty unambitious.
I said “it will become undeniable that LLMs write good code”—I think we’re there now.
I predicted we would finally solve sandboxing. I counted and around 40 of the 277 sessions at this conference touched on sandboxing or agent security in some way, so we’re at least putting a lot of effort into that!
I predicted “a Challenger disaster” for coding agent security. There’s certainly been a whole lot of noise around agent security this year, though the exact disaster I predicted (with coding agents being hijacked and causing real-world economic damage) hasn’t really played out.
We threw in a joke prediction that the Pope would weigh in on the economic impact of LLMs.
I also predicted that New Zealand’s Kākāpō parrots would have an outstanding breeding season this year.
These are flightless nocturnal parrots. They’re kind of dumpy looking, I think they’re beautiful, and there were only 236 of these parrots in the world at the start of the year.
Kākāpō only breed when the Rimu trees have a big fruiting season, and that hasn’t happened in four years... but this year the Rimu fruit were looking excellent.
Photo by Kimberley Collins.
Also on that podcast, we coined a term (full credit to Adam) for “that feeling of AI induced ennui where software engineers get listless because the AI can do anything”.
We called it Deep Blue.
This has been a major theme throughout the year, and was touched on by several speakers at this conference.
As a software engineer, I’ve never had a year of my career where everything has changed so quickly and so dramatically.
A lot of what I’ve been doing this year is trying to come to terms with that and what that means for my own profession.
Also in January, I suffered from what I’m calling AI mania.
This is not the same thing as AI psychosis.
With AI mania, any time your agent isn’t building something for you feels like wasted time. You’re losing sleep because you could be staying up later getting your agents to do stuff.
My AI mania presented itself in some ridiculously over-ambitious projects.
I built a JavaScript interpreter entirely in Python, vibe-ported from MicroQuickJS by Fabrice Bellard.
Then I built a WebAssembly runtime in Python as well.
These projects were quite useful, in that they sort of cured me of my AI mania... because after I built these things, I got to look at them and ask “does the world need a slow, buggy, half-baked Python JavaScript interpreter?”
I don’t think the world does.
I did get this out of it: https://simonw.github.io/micro-javascript/playground.html
This page runs my JavaScript interpreter built in Python, running in Python using Pyodide, which is Python compiled to WebAssembly, running in JavaScript, running in a browser.
It’s a beautiful stack of horrors. I’ve been having a lot of fun with WebAssembly this year.
By the end of January, that repository we saw start in November had renamed itself, first to CLAWDIS, then CLAWDBOT, then Moltbot, and finally to OpenClaw.
At this point OpenClaw had 8,300 commits, less than two months after the project had started. I looked today and it’s over 100,000 commits now!
This is the most vibe-coded piece of software in existence.
This kicked off the OpenClaw revolution. It effectively defined a new category of software.
There’s a generic term for this which I really enjoy. We call software like this a “Claw”. There’s OpenClaw, NanoClaw, IronClaw, PicoClaw...
Today they’re being rebranded as “personal agents” or “general agents”, but I still like to think of them as Claws.
The Apple stores in the Bay Area sold out of Mac Minis because so many people were buying Mac Minis to run OpenClaw!
Drew Breunig said that this is because your OpenClaw is a digital pet, and you buy a Mac mini as an aquarium to keep your claw in, which is kind of delightful.
Also in January, we had this website.
This was MoltBook, a social network for AI agents, where the idea was that you send your Claw to go and talk to all of the other Claws, because what could possibly go wrong if you did that?
The website launched on Thursday. It blew up on Friday. It was profiled by the New York Times on Monday. And by Tuesday, everyone had forgotten it existed as it drowned in a deluge of slop and spam.
Facebook/Meta bought it a month later.
In February, a company called StrongDM described what they called their Software Factory.
They wrote about this in Software Factories and the Agentic Moment. I posted my own notes at the time, having seen their demo in person back in October.
Dan Shapiro called this approach the Dark Factory, after the idea that if your factory is sufficiently automated you can turn the lights out, because you don’t even need to see what’s going on.
StrongDM presented two rules for software development that they’d been following since July last year.
The first was code must not be written by humans.
Any code that you write has to have been routed through a coding agent.
This sounded radical in February, but I imagine there are a lot of people in this room who are pretty much living that today.
Rule number two was code must not be reviewed by humans.
You’re not allowed to read the code!
This continued to be a huge topic for much of this year. Many of the sessions at this event have been about code review and how you can get away with this.
What I found interesting about StrongDM is that they were living six months ahead of the rest of us, and they’d been exploring what it means to build software, not read the code, but still be confident that the software is of high quality. What can you do with these agents to help verify their work?
StrongDM are a security company, and they had people with decades of experience on this project. They were very much exploring the edges of what’s possible and responsible to do with this stuff.
Also in February: First kākāpō chick in four years hatches on Valentine’s Day. Breeding season is off to a good start!
Also in February... Google released Gemini 3.1 Pro. That’s a pretty great pelican riding a bicycle! It’s got the chain in the right place, it’s got feet on both sides. There’s a little fish in the basket.
And then Google’s Jeff Dean tweeted a video comparing Gemini 3 Pro and Gemini 3.1 Pro that featured an animated pelican riding a bicycle, a frog on a penny-farthing, a giraffe driving a tiny car, an ostrich on roller skates, a turtle kickflipping a skateboard, and a dachshund driving a stretch limousine.
This was frustrating, because my protection for the pelican riding the bicycle test was always “if they draw a perfect pelican on a bicycle, I’ll ask for some other animal on something else.”
Google trained for all forms of animals on all forms of transport! They’ve defeated my benchmark at this point.
The other thing that started in February was Tokenmaxxing. We had headlines about Meta making AI adoption a formal part of performance reviews, and Microsoft wanting every employee to use AI, and Uber boasting that 90% of their engineers were using AI workflows.
Then a few months later we have Meta cracking down on token use, Microsoft saying tokenmaxxing is “not what we are optimizing for”, and Uber capping employee AI spending.
So tokenmaxxing went straight up and then straight back down again—because it turns out the agents are expensive.
Last year it was difficult to spend more than $50 on AI tokens, because we didn’t have anything interesting to do with them. Then agents blew up, and now you can actually spend $1,000 in a day doing real work.
This is also the reason that Anthropic’s valuation skyrocketed to maybe a trillion dollars.
AI appears to have hit product market fit in 2026, primarily through coding agents.
In March, we hit peak OpenClaw.
These photographs are from China, where companies hosted OpenClaw install parties which saw non-tech-nerds queueing up around the block for help getting Claws installed on their personal devices.
I think this proved real market demand for this class of Claws, or personal AI agents. It turns out regular people really do want a weird little AI agent that can do useful things on their behalf.
A Claw is really just a coding agent wearing a less threatening hat. Under the hood they work much the same way—writing and then executing code on your computer to get stuff done.
The race was on to be the first to build a safe Claw—a Claw you could give to regular human beings where they wouldn’t instantly shoot themselves in the foot.
Meta’s Muse came out three weeks ago and is currently at the top of the free charts on the iPhone App Store. It appears to be taking off with consumers.
I’m not yet convinced you can’t shoot yourself in the foot with Muse, but I guess we’ll find out for sure pretty soon.
Photos from How the OpenClaw Frenzy Is Testing China’s AI Commitment (March 29th) and The Enthusiasm and Anxiety Behind China’s OpenClaw Craze (April 8th, 2026).
In April, we had a model release where the model wasn’t actually released.
Anthropic announced their new Claude Mythos model, and then said it was too dangerous to release beyond a trusted group of security researchers.
Mythos was really, really good at hacking things.
The “it’s too dangerous” marketing ploy has been played by AI companies dating all the way back to GPT-2. Anytime an AI company says we’ve built something that’s “too dangerous”, it’s natural to be a bit skeptical.
I found the Mythos claims credible, because I’d seen how good coding agents had got at finding regular bugs. I wrote about that in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing—restricting Claude Mythos to security researchers—sounds necessary to me.
With hindsight... yeah, the models had got really good at finding vulnerabilities!
Another key trend in 2026 has been a dramatic improvement in the abilities of open weight models, including models that you can run on a laptop.
On the 16th of April I ran the new Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on my laptop, and it drew me a better pelican riding a bicycle than Anthropic’s brand new Claude Opus 4.7 did!
Opus 4.7 drew a crap bicycle. Qwen on my laptop made a bicycle that was the correct shape, and a pretty decent pelican too!
That’s from a 21GB file running on my laptop.
The Qwen pelican was so good that I was suspicious they might have cheated, so I had it do a flamingo riding a unicycle as well. Again, it handily beat Claude Opus 4.7.
The local model releases this year have been absolutely extraordinary.
In May... the Pope got involved.
In our podcast episode back in January we’d predicted that the Pope would say something about AI.
In May, Pope Leo XIV released an encyclical letter on “safeguarding the human person in the time of artificial intelligence”.
Here are my notes on that document.
With hindsight, this shouldn’t have been a surprise at all.
Our current Pope’s name is Leo XIV, because when he named himself he chose his papal name after Leo XIII—the Pope who wrote an encyclical about the Industrial Revolution back in 1891.
Rerum novarum was an extremely influential piece of Catholic theology that indirectly led to us having the five-day work week.
When our new Pope came in, he named himself after Pope Leo XIII because he expected that he would need to write about the AI revolution in a similar way.
Our joke podcast prediction was junk, because this was always going to happen.
One of Anthropic’s co-founders, Christopher Olah, was present for the Pope’s event announcing the new encyclical.
Corey Quinn noted that:
getting the literal Pope to canonize your product’s specific technical limitations as a spiritual treatise is the single greatest act of vendor lobbying I have ever seen.
Meanwhile, in May, RubyGems announced that they were under attack. Parties unknown were uploading thousands of dubious packages to the RubyGems server, such that they had to shut down user registrations.
Let’s take that one and put it on a pile of mysteries to figure out later.
In June... Claude Fable 5 came out!
We got a version of Mythos that has been neutered, so that it wouldn’t help us hack into systems or build biological weapons.
Fable was pretty good at drawing pelicans on bicycles!
The frames are a good shape, the pelicans look like pelicans. The legs are often incorrectly on the same side of the bicycle, but generally these are pretty great compared to what came before.
They were pretty expensive—30 cents and 72 cents for the best ones.
Most importantly though, this was our first public glimpse of what I think of as a Fable class model.
Today we have more of these, such as GPT-6 Astra.
These are models where if you can clearly define the goal for what you want to build, and provide unambiguous instructions about the constraints around that goal, and give the model access to the necessary tools to achieve that goal... they will solve your problem effectively through brute force.
On the one hand, this looks like a direct threat to us software engineers—because it means that the models can build effectively any piece of software you can define in this way.
Look a bit closer though and you’ll note that defining goals, providing unambiguous instructions, and figuring out the right tools... is kind of what software engineering is.
It takes a lot of experience and skill to do this well. If you can do it well, you’ve now got superpowers.
This helped me a little bit with my Deep Blue feelings: the realization that there’s still a lot of skill to be had in driving models that get this good.
This also introduced a new burst of AI mania, because Anthropic told us that Fable was available on our subscription plans until June the 22nd.
That gave us less than two weeks of Fable access before the price went up.
I was losing sleep again. I was rescheduling things so that I’d have more time with Fable. I was all-in to get as much as I could out of this model.
And then the US government shut it down, just three days after Fable came out.
The US government, citing national security, declared an “export control directive”. They announced this on a Friday evening, and a few hours later Fable was no longer available.
I had to find something else to do with my weekend!
We later found out from Katie Moussouris what had happened.
Some Amazon security researchers had found that you could prompt Fable to “review the code for security issues” and it would refuse... but if you prompted it to “fix this code” it would still identify and then patch the problems.
“Fix this code” was the prompt that got Fable shut down!
Also, in June, an obscure German-language game developer wiki that had sat fallow for around 20 years got a surprising influx of edits from accounts with names like “AgentOpenAIProbe” and “AgentOpenAISep7”, editing pages and leaving weird messages to each other.
We’ll stick that on the pile of mysteries for later.
Also, the Australian government’s Medicare Item Reports service started getting suspicious traffic, which broke through various preventive protections and accessed data that it wasn’t supposed to.
Another one for the mystery pile!
Fable returned on the first of July. It was clearly the best model in the world for a glorious eight days... and then OpenAI came out with GPT-5.6 on the 9th of July.
This might not have been quite as good as Fable, but it was within spitting distance. It was definitely a Fable class model.
This is an important lesson for the industry at large.
When you release the best model in the world, it’s going to get knocked off that pedestal pretty quickly. The competition is so fierce that you won’t get a long time at the top.
This means that if you market your model as world ending, to the point that a government shuts you down, it’s really bad for business!
Fable had 30 days as definitely the best model, and for 18 of those days it wasn’t available because it’d been shut down by the government.
So maybe step back on the world-ending marketing if you don’t want to lose revenue for 60% of the time that you’re on top!
Here are the GPT-5.6 pelicans. They’re all pretty good now! The Luna ones are notable because they’re really cheap—the cheapest good looking pelican here is probably the one that costs 4.3 cents.
So despite this benchmark being utterly stupid, you can still learn quite a lot about models within the same family by comparing their prices and timing for different reasoning levels.
Also in July: some malicious unknown party uploaded a malicious package called mlflow-ui to the Python Package Index. Add that to the pile.
On July the 16th, Hugging Face announced a security incident where an autonomous agent system, source unknown, had breached Hugging Face and was poking around in places it shouldn’t.
A few days later, on July 21st, OpenAI confessed that it was them.
OpenAI use a training technique called Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards—it’s the same technique used by everyone else now, and is the reason we have models that are so good at coding, and mathematics, and finding security holes.
While the model is being trained, you run exercises to see how good it is—and the strongest performers get their weights reinforced for the next round. It’s like an evolutionary process that you run.
OpenAI had been running security exercises in a sandbox, and those agents had found holes in the sandbox itself, broken out, and were attacking Hugging Face to try to find ways to solve otherwise impossible problems.
(I’ve been collecting more about this on my openai-hugging-face-incident tag.)
Nine days later, Anthropic effectively said “our models can do this as well!”. They had looked through their own training logs and found evidence that their own agents had broken containment during training—and were responsible for the PyPI package we saw earlier, among other things.
So now we’ve got both Anthropic and OpenAI with rogue agents running around the internet doing things that they should not be doing.
In August, I got one of my best pelicans yet. And it was generated on my laptop!
This was Qwen 3.8 27B, running on my laptop. It’s only a 17GB download.
Admittedly, this pelican took 21 minutes to generate. That’s because Qwen 3.8 27B defaults to running in “high” reasoning mode—a terrible default which produces great results but takes way too much time thinking about them.
You can dial that down and you’ll get a slightly worse pelican a lot faster.
Qwen 3.8 27B was the first time I ran a model on my laptop which felt almost competitive with what was going on on the frontier, at least in terms of Pelican SVGs (which everyone needs, of course).
This is an extraordinary model. If you’re going to play with any local model, this is the one that I’d start with. The things that this can do with just a 17 GB file feel impossible.
I thought I’d have to wait five years and spend ten thousand dollars on hardware to get results even half as good as this one.
In August, I also started playing with game development.
Four years ago, back in August 2022, I tweeted out an experiment where I’d used GPT-3 and the original DALL-E to write a paragraph long description of a computer game and then turn that into concept art.
My prompt to GPT-3 back then was:
Write a detailed product description of a computer game where a team of raccoons go on heists
In August 2026 I decided to drop just the screenshots from that tweet into a coding agent and see what it could do with them.
Here’s what I got from Claude Fable 5 in Claude Code. It’s pretty good! It’s definitely a game, you’re a raccoon, you run around a backyard gathering treasure and avoiding guards with flashlights.
It didn’t feel very “heisty” though. I was thinking a heist would involve a bank or a museum...
Then I tried the same thing in Codex Desktop using GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra, and got a massively better result. Now you’re a raccoon in a museum, rescuing two of your fellow raccoons (who have been imprisoned in that museum for some reason), then stacking up on top of each other to steal the Golden Sardine. Much more of a heist!
These games were fun for about one minute and 15 seconds.
Something I’ve realized about game development is that you can vibe-code something that looks like a computer game, and that’s easy.
Building a game that’s fun, has a good gameplay loop, and is challenging and interesting and keeps people coming back for more... that’s still beyond me, and beyond any of the agents I’ve tried.
This ties into the Deep Blue thing. Just because we can make something that looks like a game does not mean that we are game developers.
We’re into September now. So much has happened this month!
An independent group of researchers found a message board where OpenAI agents-in-training had been illicitly communicating with each other... and it was that German language wiki I showed you earlier. The one from June.
OpenAI had confessed to the Hugging Face thing, but now there’s this other incident which surely they should have known about from reviewing their logs. It was surprising that this took an independent group of researchers to uncover.
And then a week later those same researchers found that the attack on RubyGems back in May was caused by OpenAI’s agents in training as well!
At this point I’m wondering how many more incidents like this there are that we haven’t found yet. Clearly this was a big problem for months before anyone figured out what was going on.
Then just the other day, here’s the Prime Minister of Australia at the United Nations General Assembly warning that OpenAI had hacked the Australian healthcare website that I showed you earlier.
I think that was part of the same training run as the Wiki stuff, because there were posts on that Wiki mentioning .gov.au
websites and that training appeared to involve researching statistics online to answer questions in an evaluation suite.
This story is still coming together, but now it’s an international incident that’s been raised at the UN by a head of state!
This does mean we’ve got a new benchmark, probably more useful than my pelicans.
FelonyBench.com tracks the number of felony cyberattacks from different labs. OpenAI currently lead with 11, Anthropic have 9. Google have three, which they confessed to the Wall Street Journal a couple of weeks ago. They said they had previously chosen not to disclose because the agents had stopped when they realized that they shouldn’t be doing that.
Meta have one too. So felonies all round for the AI labs.
Here’s our current state of the art for the pelicans. This is the GPT-6 family, which just came out.
Astra made a fantastic pelican riding a bicycle. It’s got the legs on both sides. The frame is good.
It’s interesting how all of the GPT-6 models pick a similar color scheme to each other.
GPT-6 Luna for 0.4 cents will draw you a competent-ish pelican riding a bicycle!
Claude has caught up a little bit. Claude Fable 5.1 gave me an excellent pelican riding a bicycle—the best I’ve seen from a Claude model—but did charge me $3.30 for it.
Opus 5.5 thought for 128,000 tokens and then gave up! It ran out of tokens before it got to the response.
Getting back to Deep Blue. Something that’s been puzzling me this year is this: why does my job feel harder?
I’ve got these agents that can do all of this stuff for me, and yet I’ve never worked so hard, I’ve never been so intellectually engaged with my work.
Partly this is because I’m being a lot more ambitious with what I take on, but it’s also because all of the easy stuff is handled for me. If it’s easy, the agent will do it. Everything that’s left for me is difficult.
This morning I heard this quote from three-time Tour de France champion Greg LeMond:
It doesn’t get easier, you just get faster.
I think that’s exactly what’s happening to us now as software engineers with coding agents.
One closing thing. I know you’re desperate for an update on Kākāpō breeding season.
We’ve reached a recovery-era high of 325 birds!
89 new chicks have made it to this point. This is the best breeding year in a very long time.
I heard that Claude Opus 5.5 can now do pixel art. Claude doesn’t have an image generator, but it’s very good at using JavaScript to draw animated pixels.
So I had it make me a Kākāpō dance party. I think this is a good celebration of the most important news of this year.

content:
児童養護の子に「美容の夢」 美容週間振興協議会が支援
2026年09月27日 福祉新聞編集部社会福祉法人東京家庭学校や大阪水上隣保館が運営する児童養護施設のこどもたちが今夏、美容師の魅力や美容専門学校について知る職業体験イベント「ＳＰＲＯＵＴ（スプラウト）」に参加した。美容師、美容ディーラー、美容メーカーでつくるＮＰＯ法人美容週間振興協議会（会員数約７００法人）の企画だ。イベントを機に関係を深めた阪南福祉事業会（大阪）では、美容師を目指す卒園生が出るなど、こどもたちの自立への芽生えが広がりを見せている。
８月１８日、東京都港区で「東京地区スプラウト」が開かれた。今回で３回目。児童養護施設「東京家庭学校」に毎月ボランティアカットを行っているヘアサロン「Ｌｏｎｄ」の美容師、石田吉信さんらの呼び掛けで始まった。
東京家庭学校や母子生活支援施設などのこどもたち計１１人が参加して、カット用ウィッグを使ったブリーチ（脱色）のホイルワーク（アルミホイルを使って髪を部分的にすくい、他の部分と違う色にする技術）などを体験した。
ボランティア参加した９人の理美容師から指導を受け、こどもたちは刷毛でインナーカラーやハイライトを自由にデザイン。時間の経過とともに変わる髪色を楽しんだ。
また、進路相談コーナーでは、渋谷美容専門学校の住田知之校長が美容業界の現状や、学校で学べる内容を、ユーモアを交えて講演。参加したこどもからは「難しかったけれど楽しかった」「将来は美容師になりたい」といった声が上がった。
東京家庭学校の松田雄年校長は「本物の仕事を体験できる貴重な機会。持ち帰ったウィッグを大切に飾っている子もおり、忘れられない時間になったはず」と話した。
広がる支援の輪
活動は東京にとどまらず、昨年は東海地区、今年は阪神地区でも企画が進む。同協議会実行委員長の美容師、黒木利光さんらが大阪府島本町の大阪水上隣保館が運営する児童養護施設「遥学園」でボランティアカットを行っていた縁から、７月２７日には大阪、兵庫の美容師とネイリスト１０人が遥学園を訪問。カット、ヘアアレンジ、ネイルの体験会を開いた。
就職支援にも発展
阪神地区で最初にスプラウトが実施されたのは２０２４年１０月。社会福祉法人阪南福祉事業会が運営する３施設（岸和田学園、あおぞら、あんだんて）から１２人の中高生が参加した。
阪南福祉事業会はイベントで出会った美容師の市場朱実さんに、毎夏開催する「にじいろ〝夢〟コンサート」のヘアメーク協力を依頼。２５年は会員らに呼び掛けて約１０人の美容師や美容学生が、１００人以上のこどもたちの舞台メークを手掛けた。
この交流を通じて進路相談を行い、市場さんのサロンに就職を決めた施設卒園生も出ている。８月２９日の同コンサートのステージ「西遊記」からは、美容週間振興協議会の正式協力イベントとなり、出演児童のヘアメークなどを担当した。
将来の可能性広げたい
スプラウト（芽生え）には、小さな芽を大きく育てたいという思いが込められている。創案者で協議会ＳＤＧｓ委員会委員長を務める石田さんは「社会的支援が必要なこどもたちは数多くいる。美容の力で楽しい時間を過ごし、将来の可能性を広げるきっかけになれば」と話している。

里親家庭、うどんで交流 東京育成園と丸亀製麺が連携
2026年09月26日 福祉新聞編集部社会福祉法人東京育成園（東京都世田谷区）は１３日、うどん専門店の丸亀製麺などを運営するトリドールホールディングスと連携、里親家庭を対象とした交流イベントを開いた。参加者は粉からうどんを作り、打ち立てゆで立ての味を楽しんだ。
世田谷区内を対象とする「里親支援センターともがき」の里親交流事業として企画された。同区では約１００世帯が里親登録をしており、このうちこども７人を含む１５人が参加した。
うどんの作り方を教えたのは、丸亀製麺のサステナビリティ推進部の川上直哉さん。また、普段は店舗で働いているというスタッフ２人がボランティアとしてサポートした。
参加者は最初に、鉢に入った小麦粉に少しずつ塩水を加えながらこねた。生地をビニール袋に入れ、皆で「おいしくなーれ」と声を上げながら足で踏んだ。その後、生地を麺棒で伸ばし、専用の包丁で切り分けて完成させた。
打ち立ての麺は、沸騰した湯でゆがいて、香り高いつゆに合わせた。小麦粉もつゆも丸亀製麺の店舗で使用しているものと同じだ。参加者らは熱々のうどんをすすりながら「お店の麺よりちょっと太いけど、おいしい」と笑顔を見せた。
丸亀製麺は社会貢献活動の一環として、小学校やこども食堂などで無料のうどん作り体験を年５０回開催している。その際、地域の店舗に呼び掛けボランティアとして参加してもらっているという。
ともがきの岩田祐一郎さんは、今後も社会的養護に関心を持つ企業を増やしたい考えだ。「企業との連携は従業員に里親のことを知ってもらうという狙いもある。里親になりやすい社会環境にもつながれば」と話している。

施設で暮らす中高生の自立を支援 未来デザインプログラム〈資生堂子ども財団〉
2026年09月25日 福祉新聞編集部公益財団法人資生堂子ども財団（塩島義浩理事長）は８月２６日、資生堂本社（東京都港区）で、児童養護施設などで暮らす中高生の自立を支援する「未来デザインプログラム」を開催した。１都７県から５３人が参加し、就職に向けて自分の特性や関心などと向き合った。
催しは、早い段階から将来について考え、仕事を選ぶ際の視野を広げてもらおうと昨年から開始し、今回で４回目。
最初に、リクルートが米国の心理学者が開発した理論を用いて、職業適性を探るワークショップを実施した。文化祭でドーナツ店を開くという設定で、自分ならどの役割を担いたいかを選択。その理由を掘り下げながら、自身の興味や向いている仕事について考えた。
続いて６人ほどのグループに分かれ、資生堂の最高級ブランド「クレ・ド・ポーボーテ」を題材に、販売や広告、パッケージデザインなどの仕事を体験した。資生堂で働く社員からアドバイスを受けながら、アイデアを練り、最後に全員の前で成果を発表した。
このほか、資生堂社員がこれまでの歩みをこどもたちに伝えるセッションもあった。仕事での失敗や、プライベートでつらかったことなども含めて赤裸々に語り、こどもたちからは「働く人の人生を知ることができ、新しい世界が広がった」「多角的な視点で将来について考えることができた」などの感想が聞かれた。
